Bad Driving

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South African roads are a dangerous place to be. We look at how we are contributing to this death trap.

Unique Selling Point:
We have a lot of viewer contributions of bad driving. Showing people overtaking on solid lines, ignoring red lights, pushing in... even accidents.

South African drivers rate amongst the worst in the world. In 2017 we lost 17,014 people on SA's roads and according to research 90% of the fatalities are as a result of human error/bad driving. Drivers are arrogant and disobey even the smallest of road rules like texting while driving on adhering to speed limits.

Summary:
South Africa is not for sissies. The country is rife with violence and danger and our roads are no exception. The average driver is quick to point fingers at taxi's, saying they are the cause of our bad reputation, but the fact is that we are all very bad drivers. It is relatively easy to get the initial drivers test and from there on you have a paper saying you can drive, even though you may not be very good at it. Our traffic laws are fairly comprehensive but there is very little enforcement and virtually no serious legal consequence, so of course people will take the change and send the text, answer the phone, skip the red light or speed along the highway. We simply have no discipline on the roads. Coupled with the fact that we have a serious shortage of Code 14 drivers in SA it means that inexperienced and sometimes unqualified people end up driving trucks on our roads.

Some insurers have programmes that reward good driving (Like Discovery Drive Vitality). Anton Ossip will speak to the effectiveness of the programme (Specifically at Discovery) as well as what are some of the common transgressions. We will also take a look at how drivers qualify as so-called good drivers.

Further information:
Compared to countries like Australia our driving habits and road user safety in SA is dismal. Every day there are hundreds of accidents on SA roads and who is to blame? The Automobile Association puts the blame squarely on the shoulders of SA drivers. We are impatient, undisciplined and sometimes even arrogant. We choose our cars based on colour, instead of safety ratings. We regularly ignore basic road rules. We are impatient and angry. All of these make for a very dangerous mix. And possibly the worst is the fact that we all believe we are excellent drivers. "I can see there's no cars coming" "I can multitask"

The fact that there is very little law enforcement adds fuel to the fire. If you're simply going to pay a R50 bribe if caught with your cell phone, there is no real incentive to not use it.

Looking to interview a variety of drivers on how they rate their own driving to make the point that we all think it is the other guy, or the taxi's or the busses. The fact is we all have a role to play.

Expert:
Mr. Layton Beard Automobile Association of SA
Mr. Anton Ossip CEO Discovery Insure
Ms. Chantal Gray Managing Director Nosa Logistics
Dr. Nicola Taylor
Mr. Wayne Minaar

Press Release:


How’s my Driving?
From driving on the wrong side of the road, overtaking on solid lines and ignoring red lights – South African motorists have a bad reputation - and it’s not just taxi drivers. In 2017, over 14000 people were killed in car accidents and according to research, 90% of the fatalities were caused by human error and bad driving. With a high number of accidents and persistent road rage incidents, South African drivers are rated amongst the worst in the world.


Script:


HOWS MY DRIVING
V/O
Carte Blanche is on patrol with Metro police on a busy highway.
UPSOUND
There's my daily job
V/o
This driver has just been stopped by the officers for talking on his cell phone while driving.
Claire
You were talking on your cell phone. For a long time. And then we had to stop you and find you.
V/O
Understandably he is camera shy, as he's just broken the law.
V/O
His is by no means an isolated incident. All over Joburg, and the rest of the country, drivers are shockingly flouting our traffic laws.
LINK
We asked you, our viewers to send us clips of bad driving from dash cams etc, and for the past 10 days we’ve been inundated with clips which goes to show that South African roads are not a safe place to be.
CRASH

Layton
Based on the figures of the RTMC in 2017 we had more than 800,000 crashes in SA. That resulted in just over 14,000 deaths which was marginally up from the figure in 2016. 14,000 deaths is a lot. If we look at a ten year period, 134,000 people since 2007. It's just too much.
V/O
Layton Beard of the Automobile Association of South Africa paints a grim picture of our roads and their users.
Layton
If you look at statistics and compare them to what happens in other countries South African drivers are bad. I think there's a lack of respect, not only for the law in SA, but a lack of respect for other road users – other people in vehicles, people on motorcycles, lack of respect for pedestrians. So all road users have a lack of respect for each other and that for us is a big problem in SA.
V/O
We decided to see for ourselves and a quick 10-minute trip around Joburg said a lot.
Driving
UPSOUND
There's a trap here.
But watch how everyone slows for the trap and then speeds up again because we know where it is....
V/O
A mere 5 mins into our journey, a broken traffic light causes some confusion.
Driving
UPSOUND:
Look at that, oh my what did I say???
V/O
And even with all this evidence, we still cling to the idea that it's not me... it's the OTHER guy.
LINK
Many of us associate bad driving with Taxi's and while most of them are a serious hazard on our roads they are by no means the only cause of the problem. The truth is you and I add to the chaos on our roads.
V/O
Chief Superintendent Wayne Minnaar of the Joburg Metro Police agrees.
Wayne

No, no you see If you look at the statistics the majority of the accidents are sedans.

Ahh

Yes

With Taxi's only making up 12% of the accidents on our roads.
V/O
So there is no escaping the fact that SA has a lot of bad drivers...
Nicola Taylor
Bad drivers tend to be quite selfish, think about themselves only. So, it's far more important for me to get where I need to go than for to get where you need to go. So there you'll find driving on payments, you'll find people pushing in because their needs are far more superior than yours.
V/O
Dr Nicola Taylor is an expert in personality and driving behaviour in South Africa.
Nicola Taylor
Part of the problem is that road rules and regulations are not properly enforced. It's very easy for people to pay bribes to get out of these situations, to talk their way out of it. There's not a lot of monitoring on the highways in terms of sticking to the “keep left pass right” rules. So there's really no real penalty for poor driving in SA.
LINK
In Johannesburg we've seen increased visibility of metro cops on our roads, but are these road blocks enough to change enough to change driver behaviour in the longterm?
V/O
Most people agree that the lack of law enforcement on our roads is what leads to lawless behaviour, but Wayne Minnaar says Metro Police make a difference.
Wayne
What we find is that where there are road blocks the drivers do behave. They don't drive in excess of the speed limit they don't ignore red traffic lights, they don't cross over a solid white line, so where there are road blocks, definitely it's a safer environment.


V/O
The real problem, says Wayne, lies in a flawed traffic fine system. AARTO – the Administrative Adjudication of Road Traffic Offences Act, was introduced to deal with offenders who break the rules of the road... but it’s never been properly implemented.
Wayne
There's no hash consequences for drivers who drive recklessly. Drivers who drive recklessly get away with it because the ARTO system is not fully functional, it's not effective. So we need a better traffic fine system where driver can be held accountable, they must be held responsible for their bad driver behaviour.
V/O
The fact is, South Africans are such bad drivers that last year the Road Accident Fund paid out R24 billion – That amounts to more than R40,000 per minute, 24/7!
LINK
So, you’re buying a new car - maybe not brand new but new to you - experts say here in South Africa you are much more likely to choose your new vehicle based on shape and COLOUR than the safety rating.
V/O
So not only are we bad drivers, but we make poor choices when it comes to the vehicles we drive... something the AA would like to see changed
Layton
As a standard we would like to see the introduction of airbags in all vehicles, ESC in all vehicles and ABS brake systems in all vehicles, as a standard, and unfortunately that sis not happening with all the vehicles that are sold in SA. Going further down the road we would like to see that vehicles sold in SA are rated according to their safety in terms of a global NCAP rating, so either a 3 or 4 star rating and this is displayed in the window of the vehicle so that people can see before they buy that vehicle what the safety rating of that vehicle is.
V/O
Besides unsafe cars we also have a lot more vehicles on our roads and the numbers keep increasing daily.
Wayne
In 2010 there will little over 2.5mill vehicles in Gauteng. Now we are nearly 4 million vehicles. So the more vehicles there are on the road the more there will be congestion and there is the possibility of increase in accidents.

V/O
The number of trucks on our roads has also increased exponentially and according to Sean Gray from Nosa Logistics there are simply not enough qualified Code 14 drivers in the country.
Sean
Interviewing drivers for positions, 43% of those drivers fell off or fell out of the running simply based on having a criminal record. So that leaves you with a very small pool to choose from.
V/O
This means that an inexperienced and even unqualified driver might end up behind the wheel of a big rig.

Sean specialises in risk management and facilitates driver instruction and says that additional training for all road users is essential.
Sean
The difference between driving defensively and having a licence to drive is quite a large gap. Being allowed to drive, in other words having your drivers licence is simply knowing what the law stipulates and what you can and what you can't do. Driving defensively is applying that and using road craft to get from A to B safely.
VOX
Do you think you are a good driver and if so, why?

I'm a good driver, why? Yesterday I just updated my license and when you update your license you sometimes get outstanding fines that needs to be paid. I was clear. Zero. I just paid my license, I was happy.
VOX
I'm a good driver because I got my licence legally and I don't text and drive, I don't drink and drive.
VOX
Oh yes. I can't even remember when if I've had an accident in about sixteen years. Touch wood.
Layton
We asked a few people yesterday if they are good drivers and every single one of them said yes, they think they are great drivers.

Ja we recently did a survey where we asked people exactly that same question and the results were actually quite staggering. I mean 80% of people we polled said they were above average and when you look at the statistics of the country that is clearly not the case. If 80% of people in this country were above average drivers we wouldn't have 800,000 crashes. And then we asked those same people what do you think of other drivers and 80% all rated other drivers as being useless and bad, and people who disregard the law. So that's where the problem comes in, nobody wants to take ownership of the fact that road safety is everybody's individual responsibility.
Nicola Taylor
What would it take for us to become better drivers as a nation?

As a nation we are very stressed. There are a lot of angry stressed drivers on the road. We're about I think the second stressed nation in the world in a recent study done by Bloomberg. People are generally concerned about unemployment, they're stressed because pollution, crime, corruption, the country is not doing how it should be doing. There is lots that can influence somebody sitting in a car. Domestic stress, work stress, racial tension all sorts of things that contribute to feeling stressed and angry. And what we don't tend to do then is manage our emotions and I think key to getting anywhere safely is being able to manage the response to any incident while you are on the road.
VOX
It starts with me if I need the other person to change. If I can give another person the right of way it becomes an easier way for us to say “pass”. I lose nothing and keep on driving.


PROMO 10”
We pass other vehicles on solid lines, drive through red traffic lights and disregard the safety of other road users. Are we as South Africans bad drivers?


PROMO 15”
The majority of South African drivers believe they are experts behind the wheel.

UPSOUND
If 80% of people in this country were above average drivers we wouldn't have 800,000 crashes.

What is the truth about our driving habits?


PROMO 15”
Thousands of lives are lost on our roads every year.

UPSOUND
14,000 deaths is a lot. If we look at a ten year period, 134,000 people since 2007. It's just too much.

What is needed to make our country's roads a safer place?


PROMO 30”
Who is to blame for the thousands of fatalities on South African roads?

UPSOUND
If you look at statistics and compare them to what happens in other countries South African drivers are bad. I think there's a lack of respect, not only for the law in SA, but a lack of respect for other road users...

Every day we use our cell phones while driving and flout the most basic of traffic laws, but still we consider ourselves to be good drivers.

UPSOUND
If 80% of people in this country were above average drivers we wouldn't have 800,000 crashes.

If 80% of people in this country were above average drivers we wouldn't have 800,000 crashes. And then we asked those same people what do you think of other drivers and 80% all rated other drivers as being useless and bad, and people who disregard the law. So that's where the problem comes in, nobody wants to take ownership of the fact that road safety is everybody's individual responsibility. Nicola Taylor What would it take for us to become better drivers as a nation? As a nation we are very stressed. There are a lot of angry stressed drivers on the road. We're about I think the second stressed nation in the world in a recent study done by Bloomberg. People are generally concerned about unemployment, they're stressed because pollution, crime, corruption, the country is not doing how it should be doing. There is lots that can influence somebody sitting in a car. Domestic stress, work stress, racial tension all sorts of things that contribute to feeling stressed and angry. And what we don't tend to do then is manage our emotions and I think key to getting anywhere safely is being able to manage the response to any incident while you are on the road. VOX It starts with me if I need the other person to change. If I can give another person the right of way it becomes an easier way for us to say “pass”. I lose nothing and keep on driving. PROMO 10” We pass other vehicles on solid lines, drive through red traffic lights and disregard the safety of other road users. Are we as South Africans bad drivers? PROMO 15” The majority of South African drivers believe they are experts behind the wheel. UPSOUND If 80% of people in this country were above average drivers we wouldn't have 800,000 crashes. What is the truth about our driving habits? PROMO 15” Thousands of lives are lost on our roads every year. UPSOUND 14,000 deaths is a lot. If we look at a ten year period, 134,000 people since 2007. It's just too much. What is needed to make our country's roads a safer place? PROMO 30” Who is to blame for the thousands of fatalities on South African roads? UPSOUND If you look at statistics and compare them to what happens in other countries South African drivers are bad. I think there's a lack of respect, not only for the law in SA, but a lack of respect for other road users... Every day we use our cell phones while driving and flout the most basic of traffic laws, but still we consider ourselves to be good drivers. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South African roads are a dangerous place to be. We look at how we are contributing to this death trap.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have a lot of viewer contributions of bad driving. Showing people overtaking on solid lines, ignoring red lights, pushing in... even accidents. South African drivers rate amongst the worst in the world. In 2017 we lost 17,014 people on SA's roads and according to research 90% of the fatalities are as a result of human error/bad driving. Drivers are arrogant and disobey even the smallest of road rules like texting while driving on adhering to speed limits.
metadata.Summary: South Africa is not for sissies. The country is rife with violence and danger and our roads are no exception. The average driver is quick to point fingers at taxi's, saying they are the cause of our bad reputation, but the fact is that we are all very bad drivers. It is relatively easy to get the initial drivers test and from there on you have a paper saying you can drive, even though you may not be very good at it. Our traffic laws are fairly comprehensive but there is very little enforcement and virtually no serious legal consequence, so of course people will take the change and send the text, answer the phone, skip the red light or speed along the highway. We simply have no discipline on the roads. Coupled with the fact that we have a serious shortage of Code 14 drivers in SA it means that inexperienced and sometimes unqualified people end up driving trucks on our roads. Some insurers have programmes that reward good driving (Like Discovery Drive Vitality). Anton Ossip will speak to the effectiveness of the programme (Specifically at Discovery) as well as what are some of the common transgressions. We will also take a look at how drivers qualify as so-called good drivers.
metadata.Further information: Compared to countries like Australia our driving habits and road user safety in SA is dismal. Every day there are hundreds of accidents on SA roads and who is to blame? The Automobile Association puts the blame squarely on the shoulders of SA drivers. We are impatient, undisciplined and sometimes even arrogant. We choose our cars based on colour, instead of safety ratings. We regularly ignore basic road rules. We are impatient and angry. All of these make for a very dangerous mix. And possibly the worst is the fact that we all believe we are excellent drivers. "I can see there's no cars coming" "I can multitask" The fact that there is very little law enforcement adds fuel to the fire. If you're simply going to pay a R50 bribe if caught with your cell phone, there is no real incentive to not use it. Looking to interview a variety of drivers on how they rate their own driving to make the point that we all think it is the other guy, or the taxi's or the busses. The fact is we all have a role to play.
